{{No footnotes|date=May 2024}}
Informally in [[mathematical logic]], an '''algebraic theory''' is a [[Theory (mathematical logic)|theory]] that uses [[axiom]]s stated entirely in terms of [[equation]]s between [[term (logic)|term]]s with [[free variable]]s.  [[Inequality (mathematics)|Inequalities]] and [[quantifier (logic)|quantifiers]] are specifically disallowed.  [[Sentential logic]] is the subset of [[first-order logic]] involving only algebraic sentences.

The notion is very close to the notion of [[algebraic structure]], which, arguably, may be just a synonym.

Saying that a theory is algebraic is a stronger condition than saying it is [[elementary theory|elementary]].

==Informal interpretation==

An algebraic theory consists of a collection of ''n''-ary operation symbols with additional rules (axioms).

For example, the theory of [[group (mathematics)|groups]] is an algebraic theory because it has three operation symbols: a [[binary operation]] ''a'' × ''b'', a nullary operation 1 ([[neutral element]]), and a unary operation ''x'' ↦ ''x''<sup>−1</sup> with the rules of [[associativity]], neutrality and [[inverse element|inverses]] respectively. Other examples include:
* the theory of [[semigroup]]s
* the theory of [[lattice (order)|lattices]]
* the theory of [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]]

This is opposed to [[geometric theory|geometric theories]], which involve [[partial function]]s (or [[binary relation|binary relationship]]s) or [[existential quantifier]]s—see e.g. [[Euclidean geometry]], where the existence of points or lines is postulated.

==Category-based model-theoretical interpretation==
{{See also|Lawvere theory|Equational logic}}

In [[category theory]], an algebraic theory '''T''' is a [[category (mathematics)|category]] whose [[object (category theory)|objects]] are [[natural number]]s 0, 1, 2,..., and which, for each ''n'', has an ''n''-tuple of [[morphism]]s:

:''proj<sub>i</sub>'': ''n'' → 1, ''i'' = 1, ..., ''n''

This allows interpreting ''n'' as a [[cartesian product]] of ''n'' copies of 1.

Example: Let's define an algebraic theory '''T''' taking hom(''n'', ''m'') to be ''m''-tuples of [[polynomial]]s of ''n'' free variables ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''X''<sub>''n''</sub> with [[integer]] [[coefficient]]s and with substitution as composition. In this case ''proj<sub>i</sub>'' is equal to ''X<sub>i</sub>''. This theory '''T''' is called the theory of [[commutative ring]]s.

In an algebraic theory, any morphism ''n'' → ''m'' can be described as ''m'' morphisms of [[signature (logic)|signature]] ''n'' → 1. These latter morphisms are called ''n''-ary ''operations'' of the theory.

If ''E'' is a category with finite [[product (category theory)|products]], the [[full subcategory]] Alg('''T''', ''E'') of the [[functor category|category of functors]] ['''T''', ''E''] consisting of those functors that preserve finite products is called ''the category of'' '''T'''-''models'' or '''T'''-''algebras''.

Note that for the case of a morphism 2 → 1, the appropriate algebra ''A'' will define a morphism

:''A''(2) ≈ ''A''(1) × ''A''(1) → ''A''(1).
